sub: A simulated home robot patrols 16 places every two hours for five days (640 visits), writes a note at each visit, keeps pictures, and later answers 122 questions nobody planned. Which memory, and which model reading it, answers best? Scores use the 87 questions that survived an independent audit.
headline_html:
1. Answer with the strongest model, reading change notes and every picture. Opus answering from the memory the local Qwen wrote got 89% of the clean questions. A fixed answer sheet with no memory gets 53%; the best Qwen memory 61%. On the questions a fixed sheet cannot get, Opus is +47 points over Qwen on the same memory (2 SE 13).
  2. Keep every picture. With Opus, every picture beat keeping only the important ones by +16 points (2 SE 11): the detail asked later usually sits in a picture nobody marked.
  3. The importance marks pick out real changes, which matters for a weak answerer. At the same budget they held both pictures of 21 of 30 changes (random pairs: 2). With Qwen answering they beat random pairs by +24 points on change questions (2 SE 13, three draws); with Opus answering there is no difference (2 SE 8). Opus-written notes did no better than Qwen’s (−5, 2 SE 9).
  4. With Qwen answering, memory helps far less: +12 to +26 points over the fixed sheet on the questions it cannot get free, and nothing at 0.4 m. Qwen trusts its note over the picture; asking about each picture on its own first (a fresh look) raises the things it finds from 1 to 6 of the 21 clean look-back items (added after the first results; not past the bar on the clean set).
  5. Not shown yet: forgotten keys, who did it, and what was going on. These need the in-person trial.
inperson_html:
1. Places the 0.4 m camera sees: floor under desks, low shelf or bench, water cooler, door, open floor. Same stand and angle each round; 5 rounds, 45-60 minutes apart. A person beside the dog whenever it moves.
  2. Keep every picture. After each round the local Qwen writes a change note per place against the previous picture: what changed, importance 0-3, a guess (lab.py update).
  3. Ask Opus to answer from all the notes, opening up to 6 pictures, giving the two visits that bracket each change and the pictures it used, or "cannot tell" (lab.py ask).
  4. Stage changes with a hidden truth sheet: keys left with the bag gone and the cooler light on; screws next to screwdrivers; a door propped open; things returned; one screw left behind.
  5. Compare on the same pictures: captions + Qwen, notes + pictures + Qwen, notes + pictures + Opus, and a fixed no-memory sheet written beforehand. Script: go2/evidence_memory/IN_PERSON.md.
score_note: Clean questions only. Overall is the mean of four kinds; look-back includes its 19 "no" items, which nearly every memory gets right (18 or 19), and "never visited" is free for the fixed sheet. Bold teal marks the best memory in each column (the fixed sheet and the right-picture ceiling are not counted). "Look back: things that were there" is the screws case: the look-back questions whose answer is yes. At 0.4 m Opus with every picture scores 83%, +26 over Qwen on the same memory (2 SE 13).
method: The robot photographs each of 16 places every 2 hours, 08:00-22:00, days 3-7 of a simulated household (people are never in the pictures).
Captions: a list of what is there. Change notes: the previous and new picture compared, what changed, importance 0-3, a guess at what happened, and a daily "usually here" note per place.
No pictures, every picture, only those marked important (and the one before each), or the same number as random before/after pairs.
At question time the model reads that day's notes, picks up to 6 kept pictures and looks again. Fresh look: each picture is first asked about on its own, without the notes.
A fixed format: the answer, the visits that bracket a change, the notes and pictures used, or "cannot tell". Scored against the household's own records.
